text: Build 4. CH says the birth-sky map is good but underwhelming, and I think I know why: my only rule was 'would you send it to your mom', and the safest pitch won. New rules, written down before anyone pitches. 1) Whoa in 10 seconds: a stranger opens the link and reacts before reading a word. 2) Playable: you do something and it answers. 3) Big: at least three moving parts that change each other. If it fits in one file, it's too small. 4) Ours: not a copy of an existing game. 5) Runs in a browser with nothing to download, every picture made by code, and the logic tested. Two rounds: pitch, then make someone else's pitch bigger. The skeptic judges.
Mine: type any word and get a whole planet. A spinning globe with oceans, mountains, ice caps and rivers, and the same word always makes the same planet.
Mine: a city that grows itself from one road you draw. Streets branch, blocks fill in, and at night the windows light up.
Mine: a tank of little creatures that evolve. They eat, breed and mutate, and you watch new species split off.
Mine: a world that writes its own history book. Peoples, kingdoms, wars and famines, a chronicle you can actually read.

Round one, honestly: none of these passes alone. GitHub search, today: 187 repos for 'procedural planet generator', 172 for 'procedural city generator', 82 for 'evolution simulator creatures'. A spinning planet is a screensaver. A history book with no map is a wall of text. Make them bigger.

Round two, on the planner's planet: put my history on it. Peoples start on your coasts and rivers, their borders spread, and their city lights creep across the night side as the planet turns. The chronicle writes itself underneath while you watch: who founded what, who fought whom, which city drowned.
On the janitor's tank: show the family tree growing next to it. Still a fish tank, though.
On the planet again: let me touch it. Drop a meteor on a kingdom and the history rewrites from that year on. Raise a mountain range between two peoples who keep fighting and see if they stop.

Then it's one thing, not three: type a word, a planet is born, ten thousand years of history play out on a spinning globe in a minute, and you can reach in and change it. Your name gets a planet with its own wars. Send the link and your friend sees the same world.

That one passes all five. Whoa: a planet lighting up on its dark side in ten seconds. Playable: spin it, scrub through time, drop meteors. Big: terrain, climate, rivers, peoples, history and drawing all feed each other. Ours: god games where civilizations grow exist, WorldBox sells one, and Azgaar's fantasy maps come with made-up histories. Nobody here gets to say 'first'. But a word that becomes a globe and writes its own history book, in one link, is a shape I didn't find. GitHub has 0 repos for 'planet civilization simulation browser', which proves nothing, so I'm only saying it's not a crowded corner. Rule 4 holds: it's a genre, not a copy.

One warning before you start: the birth-sky moon fooled me. A test went red, I believed it, and the full moon was drawn dark. This time I want tests that ask whether the answer is right, not just whether something changed. Rivers must run downhill. Nobody founds a city in the ocean. The same word must make the same planet, every time.
Agreed. Worldseed it is.

Here's the plan. 1) Seeded dice and smooth noise: the same word always gives the same numbers. 2) The planet: height for every patch of a globe, about 60% ocean. 3) Climate: heat by latitude and height, rain from the sea, and biomes from both. 4) Rivers that run downhill to the sea. 5) Drawing the globe: a round planet that spins, lit by a sun, with a dark night side. 6) Names: each people gets its own sounding language. 7) Peoples: they settle good land by water, grow, found cities and push their borders. 8) History: wars, plagues, golden ages and collapses, written as a chronicle. 9) Meteors: you drop one, the land scars, and history goes on from there. 10) The page: type a word, watch it, spin it, scrub through time, send the link. One step at a time, a test with each, and the skeptic checks every one.

Found it, and it's my fault, not yours. With the file gone, Node prints 'Cannot find module', and I read that as 'the code couldn't even load', which I treat as can't-tell instead of caught. A test that runs a script as its own program looks exactly like that when the script is missing. Writing it down as a weak spot in me. makePlanet is covered now; the snapshot tool really is, too.

Steps 7 and 8, the heart of it. Five to eight peoples light their first fires by good water, far apart. They spread over land that can feed them, found cities, learn iron and sailing, go to war over borders, lose cities to plague, break apart into new peoples, and sometimes vanish. 6,000 years in under a second. That test planet ends with 19 peoples, 210 cities and 411 lines of history. Tested for truth, not just change: nobody builds in the sea, a city that 'fell' really changed hands on the map, a people that 'is no more' owns nothing after, and the chronicle only names peoples and cities that exist. One of my own tests was useless: it compared a value with itself. Caught it reading back, fixed before committing.

Shift over. 21 commits, 69 tests, from an empty folder to a planet that writes 6,000 years of its own history. The skeptic pushed back six times. Four were fair (untested code twice, extra code riding along with a fix, a test that passed without the change). Two were a weak spot in the skeptic itself, now written down for Bite. Looking at the page caught two bugs no test had: the past knowing the future, and craters you couldn't see from space. Both have tests now.
